title: Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks
authors: Shaoqing Ren, Kaiming He, Ross Girshick, Jian Sun

pages.title: The core idea
pages.subtitle: Let the network propose its own regions

blocks.html: Object detectors of the Fast R-CNN era were fast at classifying regions but bottlenecked by how they found those regions. Methods like Selective Search ran on the CPU and took around two seconds per image — far slower than the detection network itself. Region proposal had become the bottleneck.

Faster R-CNN's idea is to make the proposals come from a neural network that shares convolutional features with the detector. This Region Proposal Network (RPN) looks at the same feature map the detector already computes and outputs candidate boxes nearly for free.

An RPN is a fully convolutional network that simultaneously predicts object bounds and objectness scores at each position ... sharing their full-image convolutional features with the detection network, thus enabling nearly cost-free region proposals.

The payoff is a unified detector running at 5–17 fps (depending on backbone) while achieving state-of-the-art accuracy: about 73.2% mAP on PASCAL VOC 2007 and 70.4% on VOC 2012, plus strong COCO results. It became the standard two-stage detection framework.

pages.title: From R-CNN to the proposal bottleneck
pages.subtitle: Where the time went

blocks.html: The R-CNN family detects objects in two stages: first propose regions that might contain objects, then classify each region and refine its box. Fast R-CNN sped up the second stage dramatically by sharing one convolutional pass over the image and pooling features per region. But the first stage — external proposal methods like Selective Search — stayed slow and ran outside the network.

So even a fast detector spent most of its wall-clock time waiting for proposals. The key observation behind Faster R-CNN is that the convolutional feature map computed for detection already contains the information needed to propose regions. Why compute proposals separately when the features are sitting right there?
By bolting a small proposal network onto the shared feature map, the two stages become one network with two heads. Proposals cost only about 10 ms, and the system trains and runs as a single model.

pages.title: The Region Proposal Network
pages.subtitle: A sliding window over shared features

blocks.html: The RPN slides a small network over the shared convolutional feature map. At each position it looks at an $n\times n$ window, maps it to a lower-dimensional vector, and feeds that to two sibling heads: a box-regression head and a box-classification (objectness) head that scores whether the box contains an object or background.

Because objects come in many shapes and sizes, each position uses a set of reference boxes called anchors. The default design uses 3 scales and 3 aspect ratios = 9 anchors per location. The RPN does not predict boxes from scratch; it predicts offsets relative to these anchors, which makes the targets well-conditioned.

items: Anchors give translation-invariant references at multiple scales/ratios — no image pyramid or filter pyramid needed.
Classification head: 2 scores per anchor (object vs. not).
Regression head: 4 coordinate offsets per anchor.
For a W×H feature map there are W×H×9 anchors total.

blocks.html: This is fully convolutional, so the whole feature map is processed in one pass — that is what makes proposals nearly free.

pages.title: Training the detector
pages.subtitle: A multi-task loss and shared features

blocks.html: Each anchor is labeled positive if it overlaps a ground-truth box well (high IoU) and negative if it overlaps poorly. The RPN is trained with a multi-task loss that combines objectness classification and box regression:

blocks.tex: L(\{p_i\}, \{t_i\}) = \frac{1}{N_{cls}} \sum_i L_{cls}(p_i, p_i^*) + \lambda \frac{1}{N_{reg}} \sum_i p_i^* L_{reg}(t_i, t_i^*)

blocks.html: Reading this: $p_i$ is the predicted objectness for anchor $i$ and $p_i^*$ its true label (1 if object); $t_i$ are the predicted box offsets and $t_i^*$ the ground-truth offsets. $L_{cls}$ is a log loss, $L_{reg}$ a smooth-L1 box loss. The $p_i^*$ factor means the regression term is active only for positive anchors — we only learn to refine boxes that actually contain an object. $\lambda$ balances the two terms.

The RPN and the Fast R-CNN detector are made to share convolutional layers rather than learning two separate backbones. The paper trains this with an alternating / approximate-joint scheme so both heads adapt to the same features. The detector then takes the top RPN proposals, RoI-pools each, and outputs the final class and refined box.

Replacing Selective Search with the RPN both speeds up detection and improves accuracy — the learned, detection-aware proposals are better than the generic ones. On PASCAL VOC 2007 the system reaches about 73.2% mAP, and on VOC 2012 about 70.4% mAP, state of the art at the time.

With the lightweight ZF backbone the detector runs at 17 fps; with the heavier, more accurate VGG-16 it runs at 5 fps. Proposal generation drops from ~2 seconds (Selective Search) to about 10 ms, which is the entire reason the system can approach real time.

The RPN also generalizes to the larger, harder COCO dataset, where Faster R-CNN posted strong numbers and formed the basis of competition-winning entries (combined with ResNet backbones soon after). The shared-feature design is what makes scaling the backbone worthwhile — a better backbone improves both proposals and classification at once.

Ablations show the RPN needs far fewer proposals than Selective Search to hit the same recall: roughly 300 high-quality RPN proposals match or beat thousands of Selective Search boxes. Quality, not quantity, is what drives detection accuracy.
For the very deep VGG-16 model, our detection system has a frame rate of 5 fps ... while achieving state-of-the-art object detection accuracy.

Faster R-CNN defined the two-stage detector template that dominated detection for years: a shared backbone, an RPN that proposes, and a head that classifies and refines. The anchor mechanism it introduced became standard vocabulary across detection, reused by SSD, RetinaNet, and many others.

items: Introduced the Region Proposal Network, generating proposals from shared conv features nearly for free.
Introduced anchors (3 scales x 3 ratios) as translation-invariant, multi-scale references.
Unified proposal + detection into one trainable network at 5-17 fps with state-of-the-art mAP.
Became the backbone of countless detectors and the baseline DETR later compared itself against.
